# Object Types

After this page you can name Git’s four object types and say what a hash is identifying.

## Content-addressed storage

Git stores objects in `.git/objects`. The name of an object is a **hash** of its content. Change one byte of a file → new blob, new tree, new commit. Unchanged files keep the same blob hash across commits, which is why a one-line edit is cheap.

Historically the hash is SHA-1. Repositories can use SHA-256. Commands look the same. This book prints short hashes (`a1b2c3d`) the way `git log --oneline` does.

## Four types

| Type | Payload |
|------|---------|
| **blob** | file bytes (no filename) |
| **tree** | name → object (a blob or a nested tree) |
| **commit** | a tree + parent commit(s) + author + message |
| **tag** | annotated pointer + message + optional signature |

Filenames live in **trees**, not in blobs. Rename a file: new tree, same blob.

```text
commit C
  tree T
    README.md  → blob B1
    src/       → tree T2
      main.py  → blob B2
  parent → commit B
  author Ada Desk <ada@example.com>
  message "Add ping"
```

A **lightweight tag** is only a name (a ref). An **annotated tag** is a real tag object. Chapter 12 covers tagging in daily use.

## Packfiles are compression

Git also stores **packfiles**: many objects packed together with deltas, for disk. That is compression, not the data model. You still think in snapshots. Chapter 16 opens the object store with `git cat-file`. You can peek now:

```bash
git cat-file -t HEAD          # usually "commit"
git cat-file -p HEAD          # the commit payload
git rev-parse HEAD^{tree}     # the tree that commit names
```

`-p` pretty-prints. `-t` prints the type.

## Integrity

Because names are hashes, a silent bit flip in a blob does not match the name the tree recorded. `git fsck` (chapter 21) walks the graph and reports missing or malformed objects. Forges and GitOps engines rely on this: the commit you pulled is the tree the author hashed.

## What this buys a server

A Git hosting platform is, at minimum, a store of these objects plus names (branches, tags) plus auth. Chapter 23 is that architecture. The object model you just learned is the constraint the server cannot wish away: clones fetch objects and update names.
